title: The Pass Closes Behind You
subtitle: Twelve Names, Two Nights, and a Man at the Foot of the Stair

setting.name: Coldharrow Pass and the Reckoning House
setting.description: The last day of the road up: nine miles of switchback above the treeline with a storm coming in behind, four mules, a contract, and a snow-line that has been dropping since noon. Then the House — a black stone block with one lit window, four storeys and no ornament, built by people who cared about arithmetic and nothing else — and inside it a hall with a great hearth, a long table, a brass orrery on a plinth, and twelve people who have wintered together for years and have opinions about guests. By full dark on the first day the pass is gone under six feet of drift and will not open again until thaw. That was always the contract. On the second night it stops being a contract and becomes something else.
setting.atmosphere: Cold that gets into the seams of things. Wet wool steaming by a fire. The smell of a kitchen that feeds twelve people three times a day and has done for two hundred years. Lamplight, snow-light, and the specific sound of a stone hall four storeys to the roof, where a dropped spoon is an event and a raised voice at the far end is public. Nothing here is haunted and nothing is sinister on the first day: the House is warm, the food is good, and the reckoners are odd and busy and mostly kind. That is what makes the second night work.

keyLocations.name: The Last Nine Miles
keyLocations.description: Above the treeline on the eastern face of Coldharrow, switchbacks cut into scree, with the weather coming up behind faster than the mules can walk. The only outdoor location in the campaign and the party's last look at open country for eight days.
features: Four mules under winter stores, on a track a yard and a half wide with a long drop on the outer side
A wind that arrives in gusts strong enough to put an unbraced person down
Wolf sign in the snow at three separate points on the ascent — a pack that has come further down the mountain this year than anyone remembers
encounters: The weather, which is a straightforward endurance problem with a real cost for getting it wrong
The wolves, who are hungry and are hunting mules rather than people
The first sight of the House, one lit window, still two miles off
secrets: Coll Rannoch, who guided the party up, already knows they are not going back down and has not said so plainly yet
There is one set of tracks going up ahead of the party, made that morning, by a courier who delivered a letter to the House and turned straight round — the last person in or out before thaw

keyLocations.name: The Hall and the Orrery
keyLocations.description: Four storeys to the roof-beams, one great hearth and one iron stove, a long table down the middle, a gallery stair running up and round three walls to a landing on the third storey, and at the centre on a plinth the orrery: brass sun, moon and six planets on a hand-crank, with counterweights hanging from labelled hooks along the plinth's rim.
features: The long table, where all twelve residents and the party eat three times a day, every day, for eight days
The orrery, wound and set every night at about a quarter past nine by the Master Reckoner personally
The gallery stair: open, well-lit at the bottom, dark at the top, with a landing where a man will be killed on the second night
The iron stove, banked at night, whose ash-pan is emptied every fourth morning
encounters: Supper on the first night: twelve names, in one go, with no seating plan and no mercy
The evening's argument about the eastern tables, which the party will remember later
Merrit Doane finding the body at 22:20 on the second night
secrets: The counterweight hooks are individually labelled on small brass plates, and Ysobel Kirren knows every one by name and position
Hollis Ardwen has set the orrery at the same time in the same way every night for nineteen years, and always sets his lamp on the gallery rail while he does it

keyLocations.name: The Gallery Landing
keyLocations.description: Third storey, at the head of the stair, giving onto the passage to the computing rooms and the Master's study. A rail, some boards, a draught, and — for one day only — snow-melt bootprints drying on the floor.
features: Ardwen's lamp, standing upright on the rail, cold, its oil barely spent
Snow-melt prints: one set up, one down, the same small boot, plus a broad flat sole going up only
A servants' stair at the far end of the passage, narrow and unlit, which comes out by the laundry
encounters: The landing on the night of the death, if anyone thinks to go up
The landing on the first morning after, which is the only chance at C9
The landing on any day after that, dry, scuffed, and useless
secrets: The prints going up and down are Ilsabet Wray's, and there is nothing else in the campaign that puts her physically at the scene
The servants' stair is how she left, and nobody uses it after dark because it is unlit and steep

keyLocations.name: The Cold-Store off the Undercroft
keyLocations.description: Where the body is laid out on the third morning, because the ground is frozen and the House will not have him in the hall. A stone room, a trestle, a sheet, and eight days.
features: The body, available for examination for the whole campaign — this evidence does not spoil and the DM should say so
A depressed fracture high at the back of the skull, and other injuries with no bruising at all
Ardwen's clothes, folded, including a coat with nothing in the pockets
encounters: The examination, by Medicine or by preparing the body properly
Ysolde Marrow's rites, said over a man nobody liked, with twelve people standing in the doorway
Halva Onn, who comes down alone twice and does not explain why
secrets: C3 lives here and is one half of the confession, and it does not expire
The day-book page is not on him, and the penknife that cut it is lying on his own desk upstairs

synopsis: Nine miles of switchback above the treeline with a storm behind, four mules of winter stores, and a contract: carry the stores in, carry the fair copy of the Almanac down at thaw. The party arrives at the Reckoning House ahead of the weather, meets twelve reckoners in a single overwhelming supper, and by full dark the pass behind them is gone. The first day is ordinary and warm and slightly strange. On the second night Master Reckoner Hollis Ardwen is found at the foot of the gallery stair with his skull broken, and the House decides within about four minutes that he fell. He did not. This scenario ends on the third morning with a body in the cold-store, a lamp burning cold on a rail three storeys up, a set of small bootprints on the landing that will be gone by nightfall, and eleven people who would very much like the outsiders to stop asking questions.
hook: The last nine miles take four hours and the weather is behind you the whole way, close enough that Coll Rannoch keeps looking over his shoulder at it like a man being followed. Then the switchback turns and the House is simply there, two miles off across a white shoulder of hill: a black block with one window lit, four storeys, no ornament, no gate-house, no attempt at all to look like anything but what it is. Nobody says anything for a while. Then Coll says, in the flat voice of a man delivering the last true thing anyone will tell you for eight days: 'That's it, then. Once we're in, we're in. Nothing goes down that pass again till thaw — not us, not a message, not a doctor. Whatever's in there with us, we're in there with it.' He means the winter. He does not mean anything else. He is not wrong twice.

acts.title: Act 1: The Road Up
acts.description: The last day of the ascent, the wolves, and the arrival. The only outdoor scenario-act in the campaign, and one of exactly three combat set-pieces in the whole eight days. Its real work is to establish that the pass is a wall and not a road.
objectives: Get four mules and the winter stores up the last nine miles ahead of the storm
Deal with the wolves without losing the mules or a party member
Understand, physically and unambiguously, that the pass closes behind them

scenes.name: Above the Treeline
scenes.description: Weather, altitude, mules and a yard and a half of track. An endurance problem with teeth, run before any of the social material starts.
scenes.readAloud: "Above the treeline the world stops having detail in it. There is white, and there is the grey scree where the wind has scoured the white off, and there is the track — a yard and a half wide, cut into the face, with a drop on the outer side that you stop looking at after the first hour. The mules do not like it and are managing anyway. Behind you and to the north-east the sky has gone the colour of a bruise and it is coming on, and Marta Sull, who has driven mules over four passes and is not a nervous woman, has started counting the switchbacks out loud without seeming to know she is doing it. Six to go. Five. Four."

skillChecks.success: You read the weather and set a pace that gets everyone over the shoulder before the worst of it, and you know where to put the party's backs against the rock when the gusts come through.
skillChecks.failure: The storm catches you on the exposed face. Each character makes a DC 12 Constitution saving throw or gains a level of exhaustion, and one mule's load has to be cut loose and abandoned — the House will be short of lamp-oil in five days, which matters more than it sounds.

skillChecks.success: The mules keep moving. That is the whole of the check and it is worth more than any heroics on this track.
skillChecks.failure: A mule sets its feet at the worst possible place and it takes twenty minutes and everyone's hands to move it, and twenty minutes is a great deal at this hour.

skillChecks.success: You get across the scoured shoulder where the wind has the track down to bare ice, roped, without anyone going over.
skillChecks.failure: Somebody goes down and slides fifteen feet before the rope catches: 2d6 bludgeoning, and a very bad two minutes for everyone holding the other end.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This scene exists to make the pass real. Do not shortcut it. The party should arrive at the House tired, cold, having spent something, and physically certain that nobody is walking back down. Every later scene where a player suggests going for help is answered by this afternoon.

scenes.name: The Wolves on the Shoulder
scenes.description: Set-piece one of three in the entire campaign. A pack that has come further down the mountain than anyone remembers, hunting mules, in bad light and bad footing.
scenes.readAloud: "You have been seeing the sign since the treeline — prints crossing the track at three places, and once a mess in the snow where something had been eaten — and Coll Rannoch has said nothing about it, which is its own kind of statement. Then, on the last long straight before the House, the mules stop all at once and one of them screams, which is a sound you will hear again in your sleep. They come off the scree above the track: grey on grey, low, unhurried, spread out. Six of them. They are not interested in you at all. They are interested in four mules on a yard and a half of ledge, and they have clearly done this before."

skillChecks.success: You get the mules bunched against the rock face with their heads in, which turns four separate targets into one problem and takes most of the fight out of the encounter before it starts.
skillChecks.failure: The mules scatter along the ledge and the fight happens across sixty feet of bad ground with an animal panicking at each end of it.

skillChecks.success: Noise, fire and a coordinated advance breaks two of them off before a blow is struck. Reduce the encounter to four wolves.
skillChecks.failure: They are hungry enough not to care about noise, which tells you something about the winter these animals have had.

enemies: 1 dire wolf (the pack's largest, arriving on round three if the fight goes badly for the pack)
combatEncounters.tactics: The wolves are hunting mules, not people, and should behave like animals throughout: they use Pack Tactics, they go for the loads and the animals first, they drag rather than maul, and they break off entirely once two of them are down or once the mules are secured behind a wall of people. The dire wolf only appears if the pack is losing badly and it does not fight to the death either. Let a party that fights smart end this in three rounds; let a party that scatters spend six and lose a mule.
combatEncounters.terrain: A track a yard and a half wide with a rock face on one side and a long drop on the other, in failing light, with driven snow reducing visibility to about forty feet. Anyone knocked prone within five feet of the outer edge makes a DC 12 Dexterity save or slides; the drop is 30 feet onto scree (3d6). Four panicking mules are difficult terrain that moves.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is one of only three fights in the campaign and it should be a good one — fast, physical, with real stakes in the mules and the stores rather than in the party's hit points. It also sets the campaign's combat expectation by inversion: the players will spend the next six sessions waiting for the next fight and getting conversations instead, and that is the design. If a mule and its load are lost here, name what was on it (lamp-oil, or the flour) and let it bite in scenario three.
loot: Whatever survives on the mules, which is the House's winter
Six wolf pelts, which Wat Ormery the porter will value properly and Jory Pike will be fascinated by

scenes.name: The Door Shuts
scenes.description: Arrival. Stores off the mules, beds in the loft, and the pass closing behind them in real time while they are still stamping snow off their boots.
scenes.readAloud: "They take the stores off you with a kind of brisk indifference that you slowly realise is the highest compliment this House pays anybody: you are the stores arriving, on time, which is what was arranged. Wat Ormery the porter takes the mules. Oriel Fenn the cook looks in one crate, sniffs, and says 'the salt's wet,' to nobody. A very old man by the hall fire says 'Ah' when you come in and does not open his eyes. And behind you, over the next two hours, while you are getting your boots off and finding out that there is hot food, the weather comes over the shoulder and fills the pass, and by the time you go up to the loft to sleep, the nine miles you walked this afternoon have stopped existing."

skillChecks.success: One set of boot-prints came up ahead of you this morning and went straight back down: a courier, in and out inside an hour, and whatever he brought is in this building somewhere.
skillChecks.failure: Snow, and a great deal of it, and your own tracks filling in behind you.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Establish the physical reality of enclosure now and never argue about it again. The courier's tracks are the letter that told Ardwen his errata sheet would be printed if he sent it down — a detail nobody needs until C8, and a fine thing to have planted.

acts.title: Act 2: Twelve Names
acts.description: The first full day: supper with all twelve, the working routine of the House, and the argument about the eastern tables that the party will remember on the third morning. This act is entirely social and entirely evidence-gathering, and the players will not know that until later.
objectives: Meet all twelve residents and begin to tell them apart
Learn the House's routine: the clock, the meals, the desks, the orrery at a quarter past nine
Witness the supper-table quarrel between Ardwen and Oduya, and Oduya's nosebleed
Hear, without understanding it, the argument through the study wall

scenes.name: Supper, All Twelve Present
scenes.description: Twelve names in one sitting with no seating plan. The most important scene in the campaign and it is entirely small talk.
scenes.readAloud: "Supper at the Reckoning House is at seven and everyone comes, which turns out to be a rule with the force of arithmetic behind it. Twelve of them and however many of you, down one long table, with the hall going up four storeys black above the lamplight and the orrery standing on its plinth at the far end with its brass catching the fire. Nobody introduces anybody. You are expected to work it out, and by the time the second dish comes round you have about nine of them and are quietly panicking about the rest. The one certainty is at the head: a spare, grey, upright man of sixty-odd who says grace in four words, eats without appearing to notice, and corrects a journeyman's arithmetic twice down the length of the table in a voice that does not rise at all and lands like a dropped plate both times."

skillChecks.success: You get a read on the room's fault-lines in one sitting: everyone defers to Ardwen and nobody likes him; the bursar is the only person who does not defer and is nervous about something unrelated; the senior computer opposite him is tired in a way that goes past a bad week; and the cook runs this House rather more than the Master does.
skillChecks.failure: Twelve names, eleven of which you have already lost.

skillChecks.success: The young journeyman two seats down gets a nosebleed at the table at about seven, goes out to the yard pump with it, comes back with his sleeve marked, and finishes his meal. Three other people see it. Write this down.
skillChecks.failure: Somebody left the table for a bit. People do.

skillChecks.success: Pim Farrow's trick, or anybody's: a wintering musician is a welcome guest, and by the end of the evening the party has one genuine ally among the residents — Nan Gaddy the laundress, or Sennet Vole by the fire, both of whom will talk to anyone who treats them as a person.
skillChecks.failure: You are the stores, arriving on time. It is not unfriendly, exactly.

scenes.roleplayNotes: PLAY ALL TWELVE, ONCE, DISTINCTLY, IN THIS SCENE. They are written into this scenario's npcsInvolved and into the caseFile alibis. Give each one a single hook the players can hang a name on: Vole says 'Ah' and does not open his eyes; Doane talks too much and is always right about small things; Fenn sniffs at the salt; Ormery has a deerhound under the table; Pike is sixteen and cannot stop looking at the party's weapons; Onn corrects Doane; Kirren has brass polish on her fingers; Tace does not join in; Wray asks the party three careful questions about the road and is the only one who does; Oduya bleeds; Gaddy laughs at the wrong moment; Ardwen corrects two people and eats nothing. THE NOSEBLEED IS EVIDENCE (H2) AND MUST HAPPEN IN FRONT OF THE PLAYERS.

scenes.name: The Working Day
scenes.description: A day inside the routine: desks, ledgers, the orrery, the eastern tables argument, and the House's clock. Establishing the pattern the murder will break.
scenes.readAloud: "A day at the Reckoning House has a shape you could set a watch by, and several people here do. The clock strikes the quarters. The desks are at work from eight, in pairs, each one checking the other's arithmetic and initialling the foot of every column, and the noise of it is pens and paper and the occasional low argument about a decimal. At noon they stop and eat. At two they go back. At six they stop and Ysobel Kirren winds and oils the orrery and hangs the counterweights back on their labelled hooks, which takes her three-quarters of an hour and which she does with a cloth over her shoulder like a groom on a horse. And at about a quarter past nine, every night, without exception, for nineteen years, the Master goes up the gallery stair and sets the upper gearing for the night."

skillChecks.success: Left alone in the computing rooms for an hour, you can start to read the work: three years of published tables in bound quires, initialled at the foot of every column, cross-checked in pairs. It is a system designed so that no single person's error can get through. Which means every error that got through was signed for by two people, or by one person twice.
skillChecks.failure: Columns of figures in four hands. It is beautiful and impenetrable.

skillChecks.success: You know what the Almanac is worth: every farm, harbour and mill in the province plans its year on these tables, and the eastern hundreds in particular plant to the printed frost date because the eastern hundreds have poor land and no margin. A nine-day error there is a lost crop.
skillChecks.failure: It is a book of dates. People buy it.

skillChecks.success: Ardwen and Wray have a short, quiet, extremely tense exchange at her desk at about four in the afternoon, of which you hear one sentence — his: 'Then it goes in as it stands.' She does not answer him.
skillChecks.failure: Two senior people talking about work, at a distance, in low voices.

scenes.roleplayNotes: The routine is the evidence. Everything about the murder is proved by a deviation from a pattern the players have to have seen first: Ardwen's lamp on the rail, the quarter-past-nine setting, the labelled hooks, the initialled columns. Spend real table time on an ordinary day. If the players are impatient, that is fine — they will be back here on day four wishing they had paid attention.

scenes.name: A Quarter Past Eight
scenes.description: The second night. The argument through the study wall, heard by an old man at the fire who times things by the chime, and by the party if they are in the hall.
scenes.readAloud: "The second evening is quieter. The hall has three or four people in it: Sennet Vole in his chair by the fire with his eyes shut, one of the journeymen writing letters he cannot send, the cook coming through twice. The quarter chimes. And through the wall behind Vole's chair — the study wall, though you may not know that yet — there is the sound of two people having an argument in the way that people who work together argue, which is to say without ever raising their voices past a certain point, so that all you get is the shape of it: a long even one, and a short uneven one, and the long even one saying the same thing several times. It runs about a quarter of an hour. Then a door, and somebody going up the gallery stair, quickly. Vole says, without opening his eyes: 'That's the third time this week.'"

skillChecks.success: You can tell which voices. His and hers — the Master's, and the senior computer's, the tired woman who sat opposite him at supper. You cannot make out a word.
skillChecks.failure: Two people arguing through a stone wall. Could be anyone in the House.

skillChecks.success: Sennet Vole is nearly blind, sits here every evening, hears everything, and times it all by the chimes without being asked to. He is the best witness in this building and every single person in it treats him as furniture.
skillChecks.failure: An old man dozing by a fire.

scenes.roleplayNotes: This is the murder's motive happening in the next room, forty minutes before the blow, and the party is allowed to be present for it. Do not signpost it. If they ask Vole about it later — and they should, because nobody else will — he can time it exactly: after the quarter, before the half. That is the timeline in the caseFile and it is correct.

acts.title: Act 3: The Foot of the Stair
acts.description: The death, the discovery, the House's four-minute consensus that it was a fall, and the first morning after — which is the only morning C9 exists. The scenario ends with the party holding two clues and eleven people who wish they would stop.
objectives: Witness the discovery and the House's immediate reaction
Get to the gallery landing before the prints dry (C9 — day one only)
Find the lamp on the rail (C1)
Examine the body, or prepare it properly (C3)

scenes.name: Twenty Past Ten
scenes.description: Merrit Doane comes down for a book and finds the Master Reckoner at the foot of the gallery stair. The House assembles in about ninety seconds and decides in about four minutes.
scenes.readAloud: "You are woken, or you are still up, by a noise from the hall that is not a word — a young man's voice going up into a register it does not have, twice, and then a great deal of running. The hall fills in ninety seconds: people in nightshirts with candles, the cook with a lamp held high, the porter with his dog, all of them stopping at the same distance in a rough circle. Master Reckoner Hollis Ardwen is at the foot of the gallery stair, face down on the flags, arms out. His right forearm is broken. There is a great deal of blood from the back of his head and it has stopped spreading. And within four minutes — you can time it — the shape of the whole thing has been agreed by everybody standing there. He came down the stair in the dark. He was sixty-one. He fell."

skillChecks.success: Nobody in this room is performing grief and nobody is performing innocence. They are relieved to have an explanation, and the speed with which they reached it is about wanting the night to be over rather than about hiding anything. One person is not relieved. You cannot tell which from here, only that somebody in the circle has not moved at all.
skillChecks.failure: Eleven people in nightshirts, all shocked, all talking at once.

skillChecks.success: The blood has stopped spreading and has begun to congeal at the edges. He has been here longer than the five minutes since Doane started shouting — closer to an hour.
skillChecks.failure: There is a great deal of blood and it is dark and somebody is screaming.

skillChecks.success: He is long dead — an hour at least, probably more — which does not fit a man who was seen alive at nine and found at twenty past ten unless he lay here for an hour with the hall empty. Which, on this House's routine, he could have.
skillChecks.failure: He is dead. That much is not in doubt.

scenes.roleplayNotes: Do not depict the blow and do not linger on the body. The death is discovered, not shown. The four-minute consensus is the scenario's real horror: eleven intelligent, careful, honest people looking at a staged scene and agreeing on the obvious answer because the obvious answer lets everyone go back to bed. Merrit Doane starts saying Tace's name within the hour and does not stop.

scenes.name: The Landing, Before It Dries
scenes.description: The only chance at C9. If the party goes up the stair that night or during the first full day, the prints are there. If not, they are gone, and the DM must say so plainly and let them be gone.
scenes.readAloud: "The gallery landing is cold and the draught up here is remarkable. Somebody's lamp is standing on the rail — upright, untipped, dead cold, and when you pick it up it is still nearly full of oil. And on the boards, in the light of whatever you have brought up with you, there is snow-melt: two sets of prints, one going up and one coming down, both of them the same small boot with a squared heel. There is a third set going up only, broad and flat-soled, which is the size of the man lying downstairs. The boards are drying as you look at them. By tomorrow evening there will be nothing here at all."

skillChecks.success: C9. Two sets, small boot, up and down, neither of them Ardwen's. Somebody came up here and went away again. Sketch it, measure it against a candle, do whatever you can do tonight, because tomorrow it is gone.
skillChecks.failure: Wet boards and a great many marks. You cannot separate one set from another in this light and the whole House has been up and down since the alarm. THIS CLUE HAS NO ALTERNATE ROUTE. It is gone and the DM must say so when the party comes back.

skillChecks.success: C1. The lamp is cold, upright and nearly full. A man does not walk down a stair carrying a light and leave it burning on the rail behind him — and this one is not even burning; it went out on its own hours ago, unattended.
skillChecks.failure: A lamp on a rail. People leave lamps places.

scenes.roleplayNotes: C9 IS THE CAMPAIGN'S CLOCK MADE PHYSICAL AND THE DM MUST LET IT EXPIRE. There is no alternate route. If the party does not look at the landing floor before the end of the first full day, the prints dry and no roll brings them back, and the correct DM behaviour is to describe dry, scuffed boards in plain language and move on. That single act of letting evidence go is what tells the players that the rest of the caseFile is real. C1 has an alternate route (Ysobel Kirren on Ardwen's habits) and does not expire.
loot: C1: the lamp — cold, upright, nearly full of oil
C9 if taken tonight: two sets of small-booted prints, up and down, neither Ardwen's

scenes.name: The Cold-Store
scenes.description: The body, on a trestle, on the third morning. C3 — half of what makes Ilsabet Wray confess — and it does not expire.
scenes.readAloud: "They put him in the cold-store off the undercroft because the ground outside is four feet down to frost and nobody is digging anything until thaw. It is a stone room with a trestle and a sheet and a small high window, and it is quite peaceful. Ysolde Marrow says the rites for a man nobody liked, at eight in the morning, with the entire House standing in the doorway behind her not quite coming in. And afterwards, when they have gone back up to breakfast, the room is yours for as long as you want it, and the light from the high window is thin and grey and entirely adequate."

skillChecks.success: C3. A depressed fracture high at the back of the skull, slightly left of centre, with a curved margin — not the flat impact of flags. And the rest of it: the broken forearm, the ribs, the damage to the face, all of it entirely without bruising. Dead men do not bruise. He was struck, and then he was moved, and everything below his neck happened to him after he had stopped being alive.
skillChecks.failure: A broken man at the foot of a stair. You can tell it was his head and you cannot tell any more than that.

skillChecks.success: Preparing him properly for burial takes an hour and is nobody's idea of an investigation, and it gives you every observation above with no roll at all. This is C3's alternate route and it costs an hour, not a day.
skillChecks.failure: The rites are said. He is no less dead.

skillChecks.success: His pockets are empty, which is odd for a man who carried a day-book everywhere. The day-book is on his desk upstairs. His penknife is lying beside it, open.
skillChecks.failure: Folded clothes and a dead man's effects, which nobody enjoys going through.

scenes.roleplayNotes: C3 is half the confession and it never expires — say so implicitly by letting the body remain available for the whole campaign. The alternate route (preparing the body with respect, no roll) is deliberately generous and should be offered in fiction by Ysolde Marrow or Aldous Penn if the party is stuck. End the scenario here, on the third morning, with the party holding one or two clues and eleven people who have decided the matter is closed.
loot: C3: struck, then moved — half of what makes Ilsabet Wray confess
The empty pockets, the day-book on the desk upstairs, and an open penknife beside it

npcsInvolved.name: Hollis Ardwen, 61
npcsInvolved.description: Spare, grey, upright, humourless, exact, and entirely incorruptible. Corrects people's arithmetic down the length of a supper table in a voice that does not rise. Sets the orrery at a quarter past nine every night and has done for nineteen years, always setting his lamp on the gallery rail while he works. Nobody likes him. Everybody relies on him.
npcsInvolved.motivation: He had found three years of falsified eastern frost tables published under his own imprimatur, and had drafted an errata sheet naming the House's negligence and the signature on it. He meant to publish it and then resign. He is alive for one and a half sessions and the players should have met him properly.

npcsInvolved.name: Ilsabet Wray, 54
npcsInvolved.description: Tired past the point where a bad week explains it. Competent, helpful, quiet, and the only resident who asks the party three careful questions about the road up. She sits opposite Ardwen at supper. She argues with him in the study at a quarter past eight on the second night, and she goes up the gallery stair at ten past nine.
npcsInvolved.motivation: See data/campaigns/reckoning/campaign.json → caseFile → culprit. Play her in this scenario as an ordinary, decent, exhausted senior colleague. Do not tip it. Do not make her furtive. She is the person who fetches the party a blanket.

npcsInvolved.name: Corwin Tace, 47
npcsInvolved.description: The only person at the table who does not defer to Ardwen, and the only one who is nervous about something on the first night — which is a grain factor's letters in his strongbox, not a murder. He goes down to the undercroft at nine on the second night with the tally book and stays an hour.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep the strongbox shut. He will lie about every detail of the evening to do it, which will make him look exactly like a murderer for two full sessions.

npcsInvolved.name: Pell Oduya, 29
npcsInvolved.description: Young, quick, and wrong about a reduction twice, which Ardwen says so at the table. Gets a nosebleed at supper on the second night — he gets them all winter — and comes back with his sleeve marked. Quarrels with Ardwen at the foot of the stair at a quarter to eight in front of four people.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To not be humiliated in front of the House again, which is the only thing he is guilty of caring about.

npcsInvolved.name: Ysobel Kirren, 34
npcsInvolved.description: Keeps the orrery: winds it, oils it, and hangs its counterweights back on their labelled hooks every evening, which takes her three-quarters of an hour. Knows every hook by name and position. Has brass polish on her fingers permanently, which is either the least or the most interesting fact about her.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To keep the orrery perfect, and to conceal that she has been melting down spare brass fittings and selling them at thaw. She has no alibi and it frightens her.

npcsInvolved.name: Sennet Vole, 70
npcsInvolved.role: Emeritus / The best witness in the House
npcsInvolved.description: Nearly blind, sits by the hall fire from supper until the House is abed, says 'Ah' when people come in and does not open his eyes. Hears everything and times all of it by the quarter chimes without being asked to. He heard the study argument on the second night and can place it exactly, and he heard someone on the servants' stair at about a quarter past nine and thought nothing of it.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To be spoken to. Nobody in this House has asked him a question in four years.

npcsInvolved.name: Merrit Doane, 22
npcsInvolved.description: Ardwen's protégé, talks too much, is right about small things, and comes down for a book at twenty past ten on the second night. Starts saying Corwin Tace's name within the hour and does not stop for six days. He helped Ardwen find the false tables and does not understand what they mean.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To have been important to a man who is now dead. He will contaminate the entire investigation if allowed and he is entirely innocent.

npcsInvolved.name: Halva Onn, 40
npcsInvolved.description: Holds one half of the vault sequence and will not turn it without the Master's seal, which no longer exists. Passes Ilsabet Wray on the gallery at twenty to nine on the second night and remembers it exactly. Corrects Merrit Doane, twice, at supper.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Two hundred years of raw observations are in her care and she is not opening them for a party of couriers with a theory. She is not a villain and should never be played as one.

npcsInvolved.name: Oriel Fenn, 52
npcsInvolved.description: Formidable, runs this House rather more than the Master did, and knows who came into her kitchen and when to the minute. Sees Tace go down to the undercroft at nine and hears him below her floor for an hour. Will lie to protect Jory Pike and will stop lying the moment she believes the boy is safe.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Twelve people fed three times a day for eight days, and nobody upsetting her kitchen while she does it.

npcsInvolved.name: Jory Pike, 16
npcsInvolved.description: Goes out the postern for wood twice every evening, including at a quarter to ten on the second night, leaving the prints in the yard that will be taken for an intruder's. Cannot stop looking at the party's weapons. Frightened, honest, and protected by the cook.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To not be blamed. He will lie about the second wood trip, badly, and it will look terrible.

npcsInvolved.name: Nan Gaddy, 38
npcsInvolved.role: Laundress / Holds C4 and disproves H2
npcsInvolved.description: Works the laundry off the yard, talks to anyone kind and to nobody grand, and laughs at the wrong moment at supper. Saw Oduya's nosebleed. Will find a coat with brass polish on the cuff on the third morning and think it odd, because nobody polishes anything in winter.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Company. She will give the party everything she has for the price of being treated as a person, and nothing at all for the price of being questioned.

npcsInvolved.name: Wat Ormery, 45
npcsInvolved.description: The only resident who could physically attempt the pass and will not, and is completely right not to. Keeps Ash the deerhound. Has a bad ankle and spends the evening of the second night in the mule shed, where Marta Sull can vouch for part of it.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To get everyone to thaw alive, which he considers the whole of his job and is not wrong about.

rewards.gold: None. The party is under contract and will be paid at thaw; there is no treasure in this campaign and the DM should stop expecting any. About 15 gp of small coin exists in the whole House and most of it is in the bursar's strongbox.
items: The party's own contract: stores in, fair copy out at thaw, signed by Hollis Ardwen four weeks ago
C1 — Ardwen's lamp: cold, upright, nearly full of oil, on the gallery rail three storeys above the body
C9 (day one only) — snow-melt prints on the landing: one set up, one down, the same small boot, neither of them Ardwen's
C3 — the body: depressed fracture high at the back of the skull, all other injuries post-mortem and unbruised
Six wolf pelts, if the party wants them, which Wat Ormery will value at about 8 gp the lot
rewards.story: Twelve names, two nights, and a man at the foot of the gallery stair whose death the House agreed on in four minutes. The party has a lamp that should not be where it is, a body that was struck and then moved, and — if they were quick — a set of small bootprints that will be gone by tomorrow evening. They also have eleven people who have decided the matter is closed, an apprentice loudly accusing the bursar, and eight days.

twists: The House reaches its verdict in four minutes and it is not a cover-up. Eleven careful, honest people look at a staged scene and agree on the obvious answer because the obvious answer lets everybody go back to bed. Nobody is lying in that circle except one person, and that person is agreeing with everyone else.

The best witness in the building is the one nobody talks to. Sennet Vole is nearly blind, sits by the fire every evening, hears everything, and times all of it by the chimes — and no resident has asked him a question in four years.

The bootprints on the landing dry. There is no alternate route to C9 and the DM must let it expire if the party does not look on the first day. That single act of letting evidence go is what tells the players the caseFile is real.

Every clue in this scenario points at a deviation from a routine the players had to have witnessed first. The lamp is only evidence because Ardwen set it on that rail every night for nineteen years, and the players saw him do it once.
dmTips: READ THE CASE FILE BEFORE THE FIRST SESSION. data/campaigns/reckoning/campaign.json → caseFile. It contains the culprit, the method, the exact timeline, all nine clues with their DCs and alternate routes, all three herrings with their disproofs, and every resident's alibi. Treat it as ground truth exactly as you treat a character's hit points. Do not change the culprit because a player suspects someone else, and do not confirm a suspicion the evidence does not support.

THERE IS NO SUPERNATURAL ELEMENT IN THIS CAMPAIGN AT ALL. No ghost, no possession, no curse, no prophecy. If a player casts Speak with Dead — and at level 2 to 5 they cannot, which is deliberate — or acquires it later, the correct DM behaviour is to have the corpse answer five questions truthfully and unhelpfully, because Hollis Ardwen never saw who hit him: he was facing the orrery and did not turn round. Prepare that answer in advance; do not improvise it.

PLAY ALL TWELVE RESIDENTS ONCE, DISTINCTLY, AT THE FIRST SUPPER, and give each of them one hook a player can hang a name on. Twelve is a lot and the players will lose most of them; that is fine and realistic, and the ones they remember are the ones they will investigate. Keep the alibi list from the caseFile open in front of you from session one.

THE NOSEBLEED MUST HAPPEN ON SCREEN. Pell Oduya bleeds at the supper table on the second night, in front of the party and three residents, and comes back with his sleeve marked. That is herring H2 planted honestly. A fair-play mystery requires that every misleading fact be shown to the players rather than reported to them later.

SPEND REAL TABLE TIME ON AN ORDINARY DAY. The routine is the evidence: the quarter chimes, the paired desks and initialled columns, Kirren winding the orrery at six, Ardwen setting it at a quarter past nine with his lamp on the rail. Every clue in the campaign is a deviation from a pattern the players must have seen first. If they are bored on day one they will be grateful on day four.

DO NOT DEPICT THE DEATH. It is discovered, not shown. No flashback, no dream, no vision. Describe the scene at the foot of the stair plainly and without relish, and let the horror be the four-minute consensus rather than the corpse.

LET C9 EXPIRE. This is the single most important instruction in this scenario. There is no alternate route to the bootprints, and if the party does not look at the landing floor before the end of the first full day, the DM must describe dry scuffed boards in plain language and move on without hedging. The players learning that evidence really does disappear is what makes every subsequent roll matter.

OFFER C3'S ALTERNATE ROUTE GENEROUSLY. If nobody makes the Medicine check, have Ysolde Marrow or Aldous Penn suggest preparing the body properly for burial — an hour's work, no roll, every observation given. C3 is half the confession and the campaign does not work without it. The alternate route costs an hour here rather than a day because this clue is load-bearing.

MERRIT DOANE WILL WRECK THE INVESTIGATION IF ALLOWED and that is his function. He starts saying Tace's name within an hour of finding the body and does not stop. Let him poison the House against Tace, let the party spend a session on herring H1, and let them notice on day four that they got there by following a twenty-two-year-old who was certain.

PACE IT AS TWO SESSIONS: the road up, the wolves and the arrival, then the first supper and the working day; then the second night, the argument through the wall, the discovery, the landing and the cold-store. End the scenario on the third morning with the House going back to work and the party holding two clues nobody wants to look at.
